title: At the foot of the cross (John 19:25–30)
hook: his mother stands there, and he gives her and John to each other

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pilate and Simon: the man with the power, and the Cyrenian who carried the cross. Your line was someone carried it with him. What did you carry? Today, the hardest place in the story. Day sixty-nine.

At a hospital bed there can come a point where there's nothing left to do. No more phone calls, no more questions for the doctor. Just being there. Staying. Outside Jerusalem is a place John calls Golgotha, the place of a skull, and a Roman cross. Over it hangs the title Pilate wrote: Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews. Standing near a man Rome was executing under that title can't have been safe. But John says a small group stands near the cross anyway. Today, tetelestai.
screen: `BY A HOSPITAL BED.` → `GOLGOTHA, OUTSIDE THE CITY.` → `A FEW WHO STAYED.`

segments.voice: John names them, in the King James Bible: "Now there stood by the cross of Jesus his mother, and his mother's sister, Mary the wife of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalene." Mostly women. And one man John never names, only calls the disciple whom Jesus loved; Christian tradition has long said this was John himself. And there is Mary, his mother. The one who said let it be to the angel, who wrapped him in cloths and laid him in a manger, who heard Simeon say a sword would pierce her own soul. Now she's here. Then Jesus, in terrible pain, looks down and takes care of her. "Woman, behold thy son!" And to the disciple: "Behold thy mother!" And John says: "And from that hour that disciple took her unto his own home." Even on the cross he's making sure his mother won't be alone. Some read more here too: Catholics and Orthodox Christians often see Mary given as a mother to every disciple. Then he says: "I thirst." They lift a sponge of sour wine to his mouth. And then three words in English, one word in Greek: "It is finished: and he bowed his head, and gave up the ghost." The Greek is tetelestai. It means finished, completed, accomplished, brought to its end. Not I'm finished, as in defeated. It is finished, as in done, the work completed. Christians have long sung a Latin hymn about this scene called Stabat Mater, the mother was standing. Because that's what she did. She couldn't stop it. She couldn't fix it. She stood there. She stayed.
screen: `THERE STOOD BY THE CROSS HIS MOTHER.` · `WOMAN, BEHOLD THY SON.` · `I THIRST.` · `TETELESTAI: COMPLETED.` · then, large: `IT IS FINISHED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let yourself be still. Think of someone who is suffering right now. Someone sick, grieving, lonely, stuck, or just worn down. You probably can't fix it. That's hard. Instead of looking for the fix, picture simply being with them. Sitting in the room. Staying on the phone a little longer. Not leaving when it gets uncomfortable. Hold them in mind for the rest of the sit, and just stay. If you pray, you can hold them before God without words. The bell holds the time.
Tetelestai. Jesus's last word from the cross in John's Gospel, one Greek word meaning it is finished: not defeat, but a work completed.
Your line: stay. Today, stay with someone who is suffering, in person, by phone, or by message, a little longer than is comfortable. Day sixty-nine.

howItsDone: On Good Friday, many churches read the Passion from John's Gospel, and some hold three hours of prayer and silence in the afternoon. The Stabat Mater is sung in many churches, and Catholics and others remember Our Lady of Sorrows.

original.note: Greek: it is finished, completed, brought to its end. One word, the last John records.

trapdoor: what you thought: the saddest scene in the Bible.
what it means: a few people stay when everyone else has run, and he gives his mother and his friend to each other before he dies.
what a scholar hears: tetelestai is a perfect-tense verb, a thing completed with lasting effect, and the beloved disciple is never named in John's Gospel.

notes: Beloved disciple unnamed in John; traditional identification with John son of Zebedee. Stated as tradition.
John 19:25 can be read as three or four women; the script says 'mostly women' and quotes the verse.
Catholic and Orthodox reading of Mary as mother of all disciples (from John 19:26–27) given as one reading, not ranked.
Tetelestai: perfect passive of teleo. The popular claim that it was stamped on receipts ('paid in full') is not used.
Stabat Mater: medieval Latin hymn (13th century; attributed to Jacopone da Todi, disputed). Our Lady of Sorrows, September 15. Confirm.
Topic is death and grief; the hook and practice are kept plain and gentle.

Fresh review (days 57–74): hook no longer tells the listener 'you know' or says 'most of Jesus's friends have run' (John doesn't); the danger of standing there now rests on Pilate's title over the cross (John 19:19) rather than an unsourced 'executing as a rebel'. 'Think of Mary' and 'Many Christians' softened.
